rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yā Sīn is agreed to be an early-middle Makkan sūrah, though many commentators regard verse 12 as Madinan and some regard the whole sūrah as Makkan.
rows.anchor: consensus among all scholars that Yā Sīn is a Makkan sūrah from the early part of the middle Makkan period

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: A report calls Yā Sīn the Quran’s heart and says its recitation earns the reciter the reward of reciting the Quran ten times.
rows.anchor: God records for him the

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yā Sīn has an important place in Muslim piety: many recite it devotionally, memorize it, and recite it for the dying, the newly dead, and at graves.
rows.anchor: Many Muslims recite Yā Sīn regularly as part of their supererogatory devotions

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: A report urges reciting Yā Sīn over the dead; another says its recitation intercedes and its hearing brings forgiveness, which explains its use for the sick.
rows.anchor: A famous ḥadīth says,“Recite Yā Sīn over your dead”

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: A report sometimes recorded as a ḥadīth says reciting Yā Sīn at night seeking God’s Face brings forgiveness that night; many also recite it after morning and evening prayers.
rows.anchor: Whosoever recites Sūrat Yā Sīn at night, desiring the Face of God, is forgiven during that night

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās
rows.claim: The morning-recitation exhortation most likely derives from Ibn ʿAbbās: reciting on waking brings ease through the day, and reading at night brings ease until waking.
rows.anchor: it most likely derives from a saying attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās

rows.speaker: Several scholars
rows.claim: Several scholars call Yā Sīn the Quran’s heart because it addresses the central teachings about God, prophethood, and the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: because it addresses its central teachings regarding God, prophethood, and the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah progresses from Muhammad’s mission and revelation, through rejection of prophets and Resurrection, to believers’ and disbelievers’ ends, prophetic mission, created signs, and divine Omnipotence.
rows.anchor: The sūrah begins with an address to the Prophet that clarifies both his mission and the nature of revelation

none: Translation text only; no commentary or apparatus.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Long life brings physical and mental decline in old age; this serves as an argument that the One able to cause decline can also resurrect people, as illustrated by the life stages in 30:54 and 22:5.
rows.anchor: refers to physical and mental decline in old age. Here it is meant as an argument

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most of al-Zumar is considered a middle-Makkan revelation, directly after Sūrah 34, Sabaʾ.
rows.anchor: middle of the Makkan period, directly after Sūrah 34,

rows.speaker: Many commentators
rows.claim: Many commentators hold verses 53–55 to be Madinan and say they were revealed concerning Waḥshī, who won freedom by killing Ḥamzah at Uḥud.
rows.anchor: Many commentators maintain that vv. 53–55 are from the Madinan period

rows.speaker: Some commentators
rows.claim: One reported view limits the Waḥshī occasion of revelation to verse 53 alone.
rows.anchor: Some say that only v. 53 pertains to this incident

rows.speaker: Other commentators
rows.claim: A different reported view says verses 53–59 were all revealed concerning Waḥshī.
rows.anchor: while others say that vv. 53–59 were all revealed in regard to it

rows.speaker: Other commentators
rows.claim: Others suggest verses 10 and 23 were also revealed during the Madinan period.
rows.anchor: Others suggest that vv. 10 and 23 were also revealed during the Madinan period

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The name al-Zumar, “The Throngs,” comes from the disbelievers being driven to Hell and believers to the Garden in throngs.
rows.anchor: The sūrah takes its title from the mention of the disbelievers being driven to Hell in throngs in v. 71

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah is also called al-Ghuraf, “The Abodes,” after the lofty abodes promised to the reverent in Paradise.
rows.anchor: or “The Abodes,” after the mention in v. 20 of the lofty

rows.speaker: Some commentators
rows.claim: Some read the opening verse as a continuation of the final two verses of the preceding sūrah.
rows.anchor: The opening verse of the sūrah can be read as a continuation of the last two verses of the previous sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A central theme is pure religious practice devoted entirely to God; verse 3 says pure religion belongs to God alone, without worship of anything else.
rows.anchor: the central theme of al-Zumar is devout or pure religious practice

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah repeatedly contrasts believers with disbelievers, using questions about whether knowers and non-knowers are equal and affirming that God’s guidance cannot be undone.
rows.anchor: the sūrah juxtaposes the believers and the disbelievers throughout

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The death passage shows disbelievers’ desperate end; verse 53 then emphasizes that God’s mercy and forgiveness remain available even to those who squandered their souls.
rows.anchor: A passage on death emphasizes the desperate circumstances of those who disbelieve when they meet their final end

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The call to repent in verses 54–67 leads into the final extended contrast between the believers’ and disbelievers’ ends in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: This is followed by an exhortation to turn to God in repentance

rows.speaker: ʿĀʾishah
rows.claim: According to a report from the Prophet’s wife ʿĀʾishah, he would not sleep until reciting al-Zumar and Banū Isrāʾīl, another name for Sūrah 17, al-Isrāʾ.
rows.anchor: According to a report from the Prophet’s wife ʿĀʾishah, the Prophet would not sleep until he had recited al-Zumar

none: Translation text only; no commentary or apparatus.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creation in truth is reiterated elsewhere; here it is linked to revelation in verse 2, suggesting revelation and creation share an underlying reality and creation is God’s first revelation.
rows.anchor: creation is related to God’s sending revelation in truth (v. 2), alluding to the subtle way in which revelation and creation are bound together

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rolling day into night and night into day is expressed elsewhere as night passing into day and day into night.
rows.anchor: is elsewhere expressed as His making the night pass into the day and . . . the day pass into the night

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sun and moon’s subservience shows their reality remains determined by the truth of their creation and evokes the dominion and responsibility God gives human vicegerents.
rows.anchor: indicates the manner in which the truth in and through which they are created continues to determine their reality

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening command is a threat to disbelievers and repudiates them, paralleling verses that disavow partners and the complete separation in Sūrah 109.
rows.anchor: The first sentence of this verse is both a threat to the disbelievers and a means of repudiating them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The losers have lost this world and the Hereafter by wasting the chance to do good and repent; they lose their families as they will have no one for comfort or commiseration.
rows.anchor: they have wasted the opportunity to perform righteous deeds and repent in this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In contrast, the righteous enter Paradise with righteous fathers, spouses, and progeny.
rows.anchor: they shall enter along with those who were righteous from among their fathers, their spouses, and their progeny

rows.speaker: Some commentators
rows.claim: Some say Ghāfir is Makkan and followed al-Zumar directly.
rows.anchor: directly after Sūrah 39, al-Zumar (JJ)

rows.speaker: Some commentators
rows.claim: Some regard verses 56–57 as Madinan.
rows.anchor: According to some, vv.56–57 are Madinan

rows.speaker: Other commentators
rows.claim: Others extend the Madinan classification to verse 55 as well.
rows.anchor: and others add v. 55 to those as well

rows.speaker: Still other commentators
rows.claim: Still others classify only verse 55 as Madinan, interpreting its dawn and eventide praise as morning and sunset prayers, made obligatory only in the last Makkan years.
rows.anchor: Still others say that only v. 55 is Madinan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghāfir is named after God as Forgiver of sins; other names are al-Muʾmin, for the believing man in Pharaoh’s House, and al-Faḍl, for God’s bounty.
rows.anchor: The sūrah takes its name from the reference to God as the Forgiver of sins in v. 3

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghāfir begins a series of seven sūrahs opening with the letters ḥāʾ and mīm followed by a Quran reference; these contemporaneous Ḥawāmīm, also called “The Brides,” console the persecuted and foretell revelation’s triumph and its opponents’ end.
rows.anchor: Ghāfir is the first in a series of seven sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening affirms revelation and divine mercy and forgiveness, rejects disputants over God’s signs, and presents the angels’ extended prayer for human beings.
rows.anchor: The sūrah opens with an affirmation of the revelation and of God’s Mercy and Forgiveness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 10–20 warn of the disbelievers’ Hereafter; this sets up the extended Moses and Pharaoh account, centered on a believer in Pharaoh’s House challenging opposition to Moses.
rows.anchor: Vv. 10–20 then tell of the place of the disbelievers in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Divine aid to messengers ends with condemnation of those too arrogant to worship God, then transitions to God’s power over creation.
rows.anchor: An affirmation of the Divine Aid that God sends upon His messengers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah proceeds through the disbelievers’ punishment, counsels the Prophet to be patient with examples of earlier prophets, recalls signs of divine generosity and power, and ends by assuring the messengers’ opponents will be defeated.
rows.anchor: The sūrah then discusses the punishment that awaits the disbelievers
